issues.legal_issue: A retrospective amendment that removes a pre-emption right governs a pending appeal and prevents an appellate court from granting relief based on that right.
material_facts: The appellants claimed pre-emption on the basis of a status that a later amendment retrospectively ceased to recognize as a ground for pre-emption.
The amendment prohibited courts from passing decrees inconsistent with the amended law.
The appellants sought to appeal a decree concerning the amount payable for pre-emption.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not obtain a decree of pre-emption after the amendment had removed their right, and the appellate court was required to apply the amendment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 31 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act, as amended by Punjab Act 10 of 1960, required courts to give effect to the amendment retrospectively, including in an appeal from a decree granting or refusing pre-emption. The Court applied Ram Swarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 SCR 858, which had construed section 31.

predicates.appeal_from_preemption_decree: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a decree granting or refusing pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_right_removed_by_retroactive_ch: A legal change applied retrospectively removed the claimant's asserted basis for obtaining pre-emption.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a pre-emption decree and a retrospective legal change has removed the claimant's asserted right, the appellate court cannot grant pre-emption to that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: In consolidated claims by rival pre-emptors to the same sale, an inferior claimant's right is contingent on the superior claimant's failure to satisfy the decree, and the claims cannot support inconsistent determinations of the purchase money.
material_facts: Two groups brought claims to pre-empt the same sale, and their suits were consolidated with each group joined in the other's suit.

The trial decree gave the superior claimants the first opportunity to pre-empt on payment of the stated amount and gave the appellants, whose claim was inferior, an opportunity only if the superior claimants defaulted.
The superior claimants challenged the amount in appeal, and the High Court reduced it.
The superior claimants asserted that they had deposited the amount required by the High Court decree, and that assertion was not disputed.
issues.conclusion: The appellants could not rely on a separate, final decree at a different purchase price to preserve an independent right of pre-emption; their right could arise only if the superior claimants failed to comply with their decree.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act and Order 20, rule 14, of the Code of Civil Procedure contemplate an order of priority among rival pre-emptors and make an inferior claim effective only on the superior claimant's failure to comply. Separate decrees fixing different purchase prices for the same sale could produce conflicting valuations and were not contemplated by that scheme.

predicates.consolidated_rival_preemption_claims: Two or more claimants seek pre-emption of the same sale and their claims are dealt with together.
predicates.inferior_claimant: The claimant's right to pre-empt is subordinate to another claimant's right.
predicates.superior_claimant_complied_with_decree: The claimant with the superior right satisfied the requirements of the decree governing that right.

issues.definition: When rival claims to pre-empt the same sale are dealt with together, an inferior claimant cannot take pre-emption if the superior claimant has complied with the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant cannot appeal a decree determining a rival pre-emption claim unless the decree adversely affects a surviving claim of that claimant.
material_facts: The appellants sought to appeal the High Court's reduction of the amount payable by the rival, superior pre-emptors.
The amendment had removed the appellants' asserted basis for pre-emption.
The appellants also argued that the trial court decree in their own suit had become final; on that argument, their claim was unaffected by the High Court decree.
The High Court appeal concerned the consolidated rival claims, and the rival pre-emptors had been parties to it.
issues.conclusion: The appellants had no right to appeal: if they sought to assert a pre-emption right, that right had been removed; if their own decree was already final and unaffected, they were not aggrieved by the challenged decree. The preliminary objection succeeded and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: A right of appeal against a decree determining pre-emption money belongs to a person whose pre-emption claim is adversely affected by the decree. A claim that is legally unavailable cannot ground an appeal, and a claimant whose own final decree is unaffected is not aggrieved by the challenged decree. The Court's application of section 31, as construed in Ram Swarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 SCR 858, and its analysis of the consolidated claims under section 28 and Order 20, rule 14, of the Code of Civil Procedure informed this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_from_rival_preemption_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree determining claims by rival pre-emptors to the same sale.
predicates.claimant_right_removed_by_retroactive_ch: A legal change applied retrospectively removed the claimant's asserted basis for obtaining pre-emption.
predicates.claimant_own_claim_final_and_unaffected: The claimant's own claim is already final and is not affected by the decree being challenged.

issues.definition: A claimant in an appeal concerning rival pre-emption claims lacks a right to appeal if the claimant's right has been removed or the claimant's own final claim is unaffected by the challenged decree.
